$$

activity_context.topic_title: Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix in the General Case

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=PDP^{-1},$ what is the matrix $P?$
examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $A=PDP^{-1}$ is a diagonalization of the matrix $A.$ So let's apply the diagonalization algorithm to $A.$

**Step 1.** From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=4 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_3=0.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- Consider $\lambda=4.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 6 \\ -1 & 5 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 6 \\ -1 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 6 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ and $x_3$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=x_2+3x_3.$ Hence, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070007/assets/8e827da643179ea7b1943c875f936de99bbc9a3a01ba35fcb8fb2095e2beac80.png)
As a result, we have two linearly independent eigenvectors

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070007/assets/6ad3b3b6b8db1e15fb26a6eec89d02c886ec91a2c7bf675980d8a8f638805cb3.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070007/assets/86e7ef62c868c3456422c0d6c5e4dcfdfafba566b1c76af2a92a90ec71ca1147.png)

- Consider $\lambda=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 6 \\ -1 & 5 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 6 \\ -1 & 5 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking for nonzero solutions of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0},$ we obtain the eigenvector 

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070007/assets/38ddc9b0ce63866264f198b968f61ae7ef60174510c0badbbcc35019ecb42d0a.png)

**Step 3.** We construct the invertible matrix $P$ using our eigenvectors, as follows:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 5 \\ -5 & 4 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & a & 1 \\ 0 & b & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that $D={P}^{-1}AP$ is a diagonalization of the matrix $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=4.$

The second column of $P$ corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-\lambda I,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 5 \\ -5 & 4 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Comparing this with the second column of $P,$ we deduce that ${x}_{3}=0.$ Now, setting ${x}_{2}=5$ and substituting our values for ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ into the general solution, we obtain the following: 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{5}.$
